source.title: Knowledge Distillation: Bad Models Can Be Good Role Models
source.authors: Gal Kaplun; Eran Malach; Preetum Nakkiran; S. Shalev-Shwartz

page_placements.theme: Distillation changes noise robustness and transfers memorized information

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendices; no apparent truncation.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates whether ResNet-18 trained with fixed label noise behaves like a conditional sampler, using CIFAR-10 test accuracy and confusion matrices. This bears directly on fitting noisy labels and reproducing their effects, but is not a direct reproduction of the original random-label training-error experiment.
record.gate_note: The paper's ResNet-18 noisy-CIFAR-10 results and the CIFAR-10 test accuracies for teachers, ensembles, and distilled students bear on V1. The theoretical results and table values about distillation performance do not independently test V2–V6. Figure 1's confusion matrices are described in the text but have no extracted numeric matrix rows. The cited original random-label findings are prior work, not this study's own results.
record.test_reason: The study uses noisy-label networks as teachers and tests conditional sampling and distillation. It reports clean-test accuracy under 20% class-dependent noise, but no noisy-training error, completely random labeling, noise-fraction sweep, or learning trajectories. Its own results therefore do not test any listed version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors develop a theory of conditional samplers and prove that distillation can approach the Bayes classifier under stated teacher, margin, hypothesis-class, and sample-size assumptions. Their ResNet-18 experiments illustrate noise replication and improved clean-test accuracy through ensembling and distillation.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies fixed, class-dependent label noise on CIFAR-10 using ResNet-18 and tests conditional-sampling behavior and distillation, rather than training standard networks on completely random labels and measuring training error and chance test error.
record.method_sensitivity: The study compares ensemble and random-teacher distillation and reports different test accuracies by method and teacher count; it does not sweep label-noise fractions.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 1 reports that ResNet-18 reproduces class-dependent training-label noise in predictions on unseen CIFAR-10 examples; its clean-test accuracy is 81.3%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Networks trained with partial class-dependent label noise can reproduce that noise on unseen inputs, behaving approximately as conditional samplers.

fits_no_version.finding: Ensembling raises test accuracy to 87.8%; distillation on CIFAR-5m raises student accuracy to approximately 90%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Noisy teachers can yield more accurate classifiers through ensembling or distillation using additional unlabeled data.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 4.2 establishes conditional sampling for a minimum-norm, infinite-width, depth-two ReLU interpolant on continuous one-dimensional Lipschitz distributions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under specific distributional and interpolation assumptions, minimum-norm ReLU interpolation behaves as conditional sampling.

record.problems: The noisy-label experiment uses only a 20%-fixed, non-uniform noise condition; the paper reports test accuracy but not training error. Figure 1's confusion matrices are not fully represented by extracted numeric rows.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 1 confusion-matrix entries were not extracted: the flattened figure text does not securely map all displayed numbers to each class and model. Figure 2 reports a student-accuracy trend by number of teachers only in a plot; it is not extracted as a row because values are figure-only and the reported table already contains separate count conditions.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling, zero or near-zero training error, chance test error, and unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters.
Relative training time for true versus random labels and convergence speed across corruption fractions.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit and steadily rising test error across corruption fractions from none to all.
Whether explicit regularizers prevent random-label fitting and whether removing them harms true-label generalization.
Learning shared real-data patterns before memorizing noise, and differences in real-label and random-label learning trajectories.

record.verdict_notes: Neither the empirical noise-replication result nor interpolation imposed in the theoretical optimization establishes any listed version. Figure 1 and Figure 2 omissions are already declared in rows_left_out and do not require missing entries.

versions.untested_parts: The paper tests fixed, non-uniform label noise, not completely random labels; it does not report training error on the noisy training set or compare the same network on true labels.
The study reports no comparison of training time or convergence speed across noise fractions.
No shuffled-pixel, permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise inputs are tested.
Only 20%-fixed, non-uniform label noise is tested; there is no sweep from clean to fully random labels.
The study does not test whether regularization or augmentation prevents fitting random labels or whether removing them degrades true-label generalization.
The study does not measure learning order or compare how real and random labels are learned over training.

conditions.value: 50 epochs; batch size 128; 0.0005 weight decay; cosine-annealing learning rate starting from 0.05

rows.measure: Accuracy on clean CIFAR-10 test data
rows.note: The text also says the model without early stopping has 81.3% accuracy on the clean test set; it does not provide its noisy training error. The setting uses fixed, non-uniform noise rather than completely random labeling.
rows.check: 81.3% clean-test accuracy under 20% class-dependent noise cannot establish fitting completely random labels. Training error is unreported. Table 1 gives standard deviation 0.047 in accuracy units, equivalent to 4.7 percentage points when accuracy is expressed as 81.3%.

relation.reason: Relies on noisy-label fitting to construct teachers; reports clean-test accuracy under 20% class-dependent corruption, without measuring random-label training error or the other versions' effects.

tranche.reason: Uses networks trained with noisy labels as teachers and reports conditional-sampling and distillation performance. Neither the experiments nor the theory tests the specified claim versions.

source_check.notes: The listed rows are method-performance comparators, correctly unlinked from claim versions. The authors' conclusion is accurately paraphrased; the theoretical distillation guarantees require stated assumptions.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 with 20%-fixed, non-uniform label noise
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports that the noisy-label teacher reproduces noise on test data and has 81.3% clean-test accuracy; this is evidence of fitting and generalizing under this specific noise setting, but the training error is not reported (R1).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: CIFAR-10 test results for ensembles and distilled students
reader_labels.reason: Ensembling and distillation raise test accuracy above the single noisy-label teacher, showing that the reported teacher's generalization is weaker than these alternatives; these comparisons do not establish the original claim's random-label training-error outcome (R2
